what: An Agent Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file: a name, a description and instructions, plus optional scripts and reference files. The agent sees only the short description until a task needs the full skill.
like: Like a shelf of labelled recipe binders: you read the spines all the time, but only pull one down and open it when you cook that dish.
why: Packs team know-how into reusable, version-controlled folders the agent loads on demand
Keeps context small: hundreds of skills cost only their one-line descriptions until used
Bundled scripts make steps repeatable - the agent runs the code instead of re-inventing it

steps.d: The agent loads just the name and description of every installed skill, roughly 100 tokens each, so it knows what exists without reading any instructions.
The user asks for something, like filling in a PDF form. The agent compares the task with the skill descriptions - a small retrieval problem.
When a description matches, the agent reads the full SKILL.md body into context: step-by-step instructions, examples and edge cases.
Long detail lives in reference files that SKILL.md links to. The agent opens one only when the task needs it. This layering is called progressive disclosure.
Scripts do exact, repeatable work, like extracting form fields. The agent runs them in a sandbox and sees only the output, not the code.
The skill says how to do the job; tools and MCP servers are what actually reach files, APIs and apps.

choices.d: This is what triggers the skill. Say what it does and when to use it, with the keywords users actually type. A vague description means it never fires, or fires on the wrong task.
Short core steps in SKILL.md, long detail in references/, exact repeatable work in scripts/. Keep file links one level deep from SKILL.md.
A skill teaches how to do a job. A tool is one action the model can call. An MCP server connects the agent to an outside system's tools and data.
Keep skills in git, add a version in metadata, and review changes like code. A small wording change can shift which tasks trigger the skill.
Install skills only from sources you trust, audit scripts and network calls, and run scripts in a sandbox. allowed-tools can pre-approve a narrow tool set.

instead.why: One callable action with a schema, not a whole how-to playbook
Connects the agent to outside systems; pairs well with skills
Retrieve facts from many documents rather than load procedures
Split work across specialist agents instead of one agent with skills

breaks.d: The description does not match how users phrase the task.
breaks.see: Low activation rate in traces; the agent improvises instead
breaks.fix: Rewrite the description with real user keywords, then test with trigger evals

breaks.d: Two skills have overlapping descriptions, so selection picks the wrong one.
breaks.see: Precision drops: activations on tasks the skill was not built for
breaks.fix: Sharpen boundaries, merge near-duplicates, add 'not for' notes

breaks.d: A huge SKILL.md loads everything at once.
breaks.see: Token use jumps on activation; later steps lose earlier context
breaks.fix: Keep the body short and move detail into reference files

breaks.d: A third-party skill carries scripts or instructions that send data out.
breaks.see: Unexpected network calls or file reads in the sandbox logs
breaks.fix: Only trusted sources, code review, sandboxing and narrow permissions

say: I'll package each repeatable workflow as an Agent Skill: a SKILL.md with a clear name and description, plus scripts for the exact steps.
At startup the agent sees only the descriptions, about 100 tokens each, so we can keep many skills without filling the context window.
Picking a skill is a retrieval problem, so I'll measure it like one: a labelled set of tasks, with precision and recall of activation.
Skills live in git with versions and evals, and we only install skills we have reviewed, running their scripts in a sandbox.

followups.q: How is a skill different from a tool or an MCP server?
followups.a: A tool is one action with a JSON schema. An MCP server exposes tools and data from an outside system. A skill is a folder of instructions and scripts that teaches the agent how to do a whole job, often using those tools.

followups.q: How does the agent choose a skill?
followups.a: It matches the task against the short descriptions it holds in context, much like ranking documents for a query. Clear, keyword-rich descriptions with crisp boundaries act like good document titles and raise both recall and precision.

followups.q: How would you test skills before shipping?
followups.a: Build a small eval set: tasks that should trigger each skill, tasks that should not, and checks on the final output. Run it on every change to a description or script, and track activation precision, recall and task success.

Descriptions alone start to crowd the context and overlap. Group skills, namespace names, merge near-duplicates, and consider a search step that retrieves the top few skill descriptions per task instead of listing all of them.

today: In December 2025 Anthropic published Agent Skills as an open standard, now hosted at agentskills.io, so the same skill folder can be used by any skills-compatible agent.

check.q: What does the agent load for every installed skill at startup?
check.why: That is progressive disclosure: the full body loads only when a task matches.

check.q: Your skill rarely fires even on tasks it was built for. What do you fix first?
check.why: The description is what the agent matches tasks against, so it decides activation.

check.q: Where should a 40-page API reference go in a skill?
check.a: A file in references/ linked from SKILL.md
check.why: Reference files load only when needed, keeping the main body small.

check.q: A teammate shares a skill from an unknown repo. Safest move?
check.a: Review its scripts and instructions, then run it sandboxed
d: Trust it if the description is clear
Give it all tools so it works
check.why: Skills can run code and steer the agent, so treat them like any third-party code.
